title: The Feature Blame

scenario.situation: The churn model flags support-ticket count as the single most important feature. Leadership wants to reduce ticket volume — by simplifying the help portal, limiting ticket categories, and auto-closing old tickets — to drive churn down.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Head of Product is convinced that support tickets cause churn, so suppressing ticket volume will reduce it.
scenario.question: Is feature importance the right signal to act on here?

decisions.prompt: The Head of Product wants an action plan by end of week. How do you frame your investigation before recommending anything?

options.label: Optimize the help portal to reduce inbound tickets
options.detail: Accept the model's signal at face value and design A/B tests around reducing ticket volume.
options.consequence: You've taken the model's importance score as a causal recipe and skipped diagnosis entirely. If tickets are a symptom, suppressing them leaves the root cause intact — and you won't know until churn fails to improve.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the stakeholder's intervention before understanding what tickets represent.

options.label: Segment churners by ticket behavior to find what they actually have in common
options.detail: Before acting, slice churned users by ticket volume, ticket topic, and product-usage patterns to see whether tickets are the problem or a signal of something deeper.
options.consequence: Segmenting reveals that high-ticket churners share specific product-area complaints — the tickets are a trace of friction, not its cause. Now you have a thread worth pulling.

options.label: Re-run the model with ticket count removed to see if churn predictions degrade
options.detail: Drop the feature and check how much model accuracy drops.
options.consequence: Accuracy barely drops — the model redistributes importance to correlated proxies. This tells you nothing about whether intervening on tickets changes churn behavior.
options.divergenceCost: Confused feature redundancy with causal irrelevance — the wrong test for this question.

options.label: Survey high-ticket users and ask if support frustration made them consider leaving
options.detail: Run a quick NPS/exit survey targeting users who submitted many tickets.
options.consequence: Users say support was frustrating — but they also mention product bugs and missing features. The survey conflates the symptom with the cause and can't isolate which to fix first.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a self-report instrument that can't separate symptom from cause.

decisions.prompt: You've segmented churners by ticket volume. Which metric do you use to judge whether tickets are the real problem?

artifact.title: Churned users by ticket-volume bucket — last quarter
artifact.caption: Raw counts of churned users per ticket bucket. The 1–2 bucket looks biggest — but these buckets are very different sizes in the overall user base.

options.label: Raw count of churned users in each ticket bucket
options.detail: Count how many churned users fall into each ticket-volume group.
options.consequence: The 1–2 ticket bucket has the most churned users — so it looks like even modest ticket use is the danger zone. But this bucket is also by far the largest in the user base. You're reading population size, not churn risk.
options.divergenceCost: Read raw counts across unequal cohorts — mistook group size for elevated risk.

options.label: Churn rate within each ticket bucket, broken out by ticket topic
options.detail: Compute churn as a % within each bucket, then break the high-churn bucket down by what users were actually complaining about.
options.consequence: Normalized, the 6+ ticket group has a dramatically higher churn rate — but only when those tickets concern a specific product area (data-sync errors). Users with 6+ tickets about billing or onboarding churn at near-average rates. Tickets aren't the driver; a broken product feature is.

artifact.title: Churn RATE by ticket bucket and topic (% within group)
artifact.caption: Only the data-sync complaint cluster shows extreme churn. High ticket count alone is not the driver — the underlying product failure is.

decisions.prompt: Data-sync error tickets correlate strongly with churn. What do you tell the Head of Product?

options.label: "Tickets cause churn — fix the data-sync bug and churn will drop."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend engineering prioritize the bug immediately.
options.consequence: You've turned a correlation into a prescription. The bug may be one factor among several — or users who hit sync errors may differ in other ways (plan type, integration complexity). If the fix ships and churn barely moves, credibility is lost.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation from correlation — skipped the step that earns confidence.

options.label: "Suppressing tickets isn't the lever — feature importance predicts, it doesn't prescribe. Data-sync errors are the strongest correlate of churn; let's run a targeted holdout to confirm before re-routing engineering resources."
options.detail: Reframe the importance-as-cause mistake, present the segmentation finding, and propose a confirmatory test.
options.consequence: You've corrected the mental model (importance ≠ causation), surfaced a sharper hypothesis (the sync bug), and proposed a path to certainty before committing engineering. The Head of Product now has a better question — and so does the team.

insight: Support-ticket count is a powerful predictor precisely because it is a reliable symptom of product pain — not because contacting support makes users leave. Feature importance measures a variable's ability to discriminate outcomes in historical data; it says nothing about what happens when you intervene on that variable. The real driver here was a broken data-sync feature, visible only after normalizing churn rates and breaking out ticket topics. The lesson: before acting on a model's top feature, ask whether you can suppress it independently of its cause — and if you can't, you're looking at a proxy, not a lever.
